source.title: A is for Absorption: Studying Feature Splitting and Absorption in Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: David Chanin; James Wilken-Smith; Tomás Dulka; Hardik Bhatnagar; Satvik Golechha; J. Bloom

record.tranche_reason: The study empirically tests whether SAE features recover and fully track information in LLM activations, using spelling probes and causal ablations rather than the original superposition measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Toy Models of Superposition as background but does not test its more-features-than-dimensions geometry. Its toy experiments test hierarchical-feature absorption in SAEs, not superposition capacity or geometry. Reported figure-only curves are recorded as aggregate results where the text describes their trend; no values were estimated from plots.
record.test_reason: The study tests whether SAE latents in Gemma-2-2B, Llama 3.2 1B and Qwen2 0.5B fully track a known feature (first letter). It reports that seemingly monosemantic latents have systematic false negatives due to feature absorption. These are direct results against the completeness of dictionary features (V5) and qualify how well SAEs recover LLM features (V4). The method (probes, ablations, absorption rate) differs from the original, and the results argue a version needs restating, so T5 fits better than T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state absorption occurred in every LLM SAE they tested. They give an analytical proof that absorption lowers sparsity loss under hierarchy. They call their absorption metric a conservative underestimate.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE probing, feature ablation, and spelling-task measurements rather than the original superposition toy-model geometry and phase-transition analyses.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported results vary with SAE L0, width, layer, letter, and SAE architecture. The absorption metric is causally applicable only through layer 17 for Gemma-2-2B on this task.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy SAEs with orthogonal features (fewer than dimensions), hierarchical co-occurrence produces absorption. It also produces partial absorption under magnitude variance or imperfect co-occurrence, and absorption in a batch TopK SAE. Independent features are recovered perfectly. An analytical proof shows absorption lowers the sparsity loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE sparsity objectives favor absorbing a parent feature into child latents whenever features form a hierarchy.

record.peer_reviewed: NeurIPS 2025 (39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)
record.problems: Most absorption-rate results are shown as plots without exact numeric values or uncertainty estimates. The causal absorption metric is conservative, depends on manually chosen thresholds, misses partial absorption and multiple absorbing latents, and cannot establish causal effects past layer 17 for Gemma-2-2B. The paper notes compute constraints and trains only a small number of non-JumpReLU SAEs.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported per-letter or per-layer numeric rows were extractable from the aggregate plots; exact values are not stated. Figure 14's intervention results concern editing first-letter predictions, not the listed versions' feature recovery or feature-unit claims, so they were not included.

untested.parts: Toy setups use 4 or 12 orthogonal features in 50 dims (fewer features than dimensions). No superposition geometry or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
No test of neuron polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
No test of origins of neuron polysemanticity.
Only first-letter features are tested; recovery of other concept types is not tested.
Stability across SAE training seeds and canonicality across methods or models are not tested. Only completeness (recall) on first-letter features is tested.
Not tested; Engels et al. on multidimensional features is only cited.

missing.what: For most letters, one or two outlier SAE latents clearly align with the LR probe, showing the sparse first-letter features are recoverable.

Feature splitting: the mean number of splits per letter rises with sparsity (Fig. 8b), and an L latent splits into upper- and lowercase latents. Latent granularity therefore depends on SAE hyperparameters.
Per-letter absorption rate varies widely across SAEs, and the best L0 for F1 differs by letter.
Editing first-letter latents changes model predictions, with partial success that is best at L0 75–150 and for 16k-width SAEs.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source. R5 has a k=2 (text) vs k=12 (caption) inconsistency in the paper. Most LLM results are figure-only, without exact numbers or uncertainty. The absorption metric uses hand-chosen thresholds and only applies through layer 17 in Gemma-2-2B.

versions.untested_parts: The toy setups do not have more features than representation dimensions, and do not test the claimed superposition geometry or sparsity-dependent transition.

The study concerns SAE latents and feature absorption, not whether LLM neurons become polysemantic because features compete for network capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
The study does not test why LLM neurons are polysemantic or whether polysemanticity occurs without capacity pressure.
The study tests recovery of first-letter information by SAE latents, not broad feature recovery across concepts, tasks, or all LLM representations.

The study tests whether SAE latents completely track first-letter information in its spelling task; it does not test stability across runs or whether SAE features are canonical units across methods or models.
The study does not test whether the underlying model features are one-dimensional or multidimensional.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE (50-dimensional representation)
rows.size_stated: 4 true features; 50-dimensional representation; SAE with 4 latents
rows.operation_detail: Trained an SAE on independently firing orthogonal toy features and compared learned encoder and decoder directions with the true features.

conditions.value: feature 0 probability 0.25; features 1, 2, and 3 probability 0.05; independent

rows.measure: Recovery of true feature directions and feature segmentation
rows.value: The SAE perfectly recovered the features, learning one latent per true feature.
rows.note: Control condition for the hierarchical co-occurrence toy experiment; it does not test the superposition claim because the feature count is below the representation dimension.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE (50-dimensional representation)
rows.size_stated: 4 true features; 50-dimensional representation; SAE with 4 latents
rows.operation_detail: Compared learned encoder and decoder directions with true features when one feature only fired alongside its parent.

conditions.value: feature 1 fires only when feature 0 fires; feature 1 fires in 5% of activations

rows.value: The feature-0 encoder latent stopped firing when feature 1 was active; the feature-1 latent absorbed the feature-0 direction. Features 2 and 3 remained correctly represented.
rows.note: This is a toy SAE absorption result, not a test of superposition with more features than dimensions.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE (50-dimensional representation)
rows.size_stated: 4 true features; 50-dimensional representation; SAE with 4 latents
rows.operation_detail: Varied the parent feature's firing magnitude while retaining hierarchical co-occurrence.

conditions.value: feature 1 only fires when feature 0 fires

rows.measure: Feature-0 latent activation under joint feature firing
rows.value: The feature-0 latent fired weakly when both features had magnitude 1.0 and fully turned off when the parent magnitude was 0.75.
rows.note: The authors call this partial absorption.

rows.subject: 4-feature toy SAE (50-dimensional representation)
rows.size_stated: 4 true features; 50-dimensional representation; SAE with 4 latents
rows.operation_detail: Relaxed perfect hierarchical co-occurrence so the child could sometimes fire without its parent.

conditions.value: feature 1 fires with feature 0 95% of the time and can fire on its own 5% of the time

rows.measure: Encoder and decoder alignment and feature-0 latent activations
rows.value: The SAE showed a weaker absorption pattern; the feature-0 latent fired at noticeably lower magnitude when feature 1 was also active.
rows.note: The authors describe this as partial absorption despite imperfect co-occurrence.

rows.subject: 12-feature toy SAE
rows.size_stated: 12 mutually orthogonal true features; SAE with 12 latents
rows.operation_detail: Trained a batch TopK SAE and compared encoder/decoder directions with true features.

conditions.value: features 2–11 fire independently with probability 0.15; feature 0 probability 0.4; feature 1 probability 0.6 only if feature 0 fires

rows.value: The authors report a clear absorption pattern between the latents tracking features 0 and 1, despite the lack of an L1 loss term.
rows.note: The appendix text says the figure uses batch TopK k=2; the figure caption says k=12. The record preserves the text's conflicting settings rather than resolving them.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Compared first-letter linear-probe performance with the SAE encoder latent most cosine-aligned to the probe.

conditions.value: Gemma Scope residual-stream SAEs, widths 16k and 65k

rows.baseline: Linear probe; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Figure only; the text states that no SAE matched linear-probe performance.
rows.note: Aggregate across tested letters and plotted SAE settings; the paper describes substantial variation among SAEs.
rows.check: The role should be main, not comparator: the LR probe is the baseline, and the SAE latent F1 is the measured value. The text says no SAE matches the LR probe, which also bears on V5 completeness.

source_check.correct: Role should be main: SAE latent performance is the measured result; the LR probe is the comparator.
source_check.problem: The comparator role is incorrect; the value, baseline, conditions and partial state are supported.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured first-letter F1 for the top probe-aligned SAE latent across SAE sparsity settings.

conditions.value: swept; exact plotted values not stated

rows.baseline: Linear-probe reference shown in the plots; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Figure only; the text says feature performance depends strongly on L0, with the cleanest features at L0 near 25–50 in layers 0–12 and near 50–100 in layers 13–25.
rows.note: The stated L0 ranges describe where the plots show the cleanest first-letter features, not an optimum for every letter.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured precision and recall of the top probe-aligned SAE latent for first-letter classification.

conditions.value: mean across letters and tested SAEs

rows.value: Figure only; low-L0 SAEs tend toward high precision and low recall, while high-L0 SAEs tend toward low precision and high recall.
rows.note: The text cautions that the apparent aggregate L0 pattern varies by letter.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated the layer 3 Gemma Scope SAE latent selected as the apparent classifier for “starts with S.”
rows.measure: F1 score and activation on positive examples
rows.value: F1 0.81; the latent fails to activate on the token _short.
rows.note: This provides evidence of useful but incomplete feature recovery.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured decoder alignment with the first-letter S linear-probe direction.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity with the S probe and activation magnitude
rows.value: Latent 1085 cosine similarity 0.12; it activates at about 5 times the magnitude of latent 6510 on _short.
rows.note: The paper interprets latent 1085 as absorbing a component of the S direction on this token.
rows.check: The row measures absorption (observed), but against V5 it shows the main 'starts with S' latent 6510 does not completely track the feature. Latent 1085 (cos 0.12) supplies the direction on _short. Completeness is absent here. It does not measure V4 recovery, so drop the V4 link.

source_check.locator_found: Section 5.2, Figure 6b and paragraphs immediately following Figure 7.
source_check.problem: The fivefold activation comparison is stated in the source, but conflicts with its statement that latent 6510 does not activate on _short.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Ablated SAE latents for _short, then repeated the ablation after projecting the S-probe direction out of latent 1085.

conditions.value: correct-letter logit minus mean incorrect-letter logit

rows.measure: Change in first-letter metric under latent ablation
rows.baseline: Unablated SAE-inserted model; numeric value not stated
rows.value: Ablating latent 1085 had a dramatically larger effect than other latents; after projecting out its probe component, latent 1085 no longer had a significant ablation effect.
rows.note: The authors conclude that the probe-aligned component of latent 1085 is causally responsible for the spelling behavior.
rows.check: The ablation shows the S feature on _short is carried by token-aligned latent 1085, not the apparent S latent. Against V5, completeness is absent. Drop V4, since this is a causal check of absorption, not of feature recovery.

source_check.locator_found: Section 4, SAE error-term treatment and logit metric; Section 5.2, Figure 7 and accompanying paragraphs.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Estimated absorption rate using feature-split latents, false negatives, and integrated-gradients ablation.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports higher absorption rates with higher sparsity and wider SAEs.
rows.note: The metric is limited to cases where the main feature latents are fully inactive and one absorbing latent has a dominant ablation effect.
rows.check: Absorption rate measures failures of latent completeness, not SAE recovery of features, so drop V4. Mean rates up to roughly 0.35 are figure-only. Rates rise with sparsity and width, so completeness fails in a substantial but incomplete fraction of cases.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Estimated absorption rate across layers using the paper's causal absorption metric.
rows.measure: Mean feature absorption rate by layer
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports no obvious pattern in absorption rate by layer.
rows.note: The metric cannot establish causal absorption beyond layer 17 for Gemma-2-2B.
rows.check: Same as R12: this is a completeness measure, so drop V4. The text reports no obvious layer pattern over layers 0–17.

rows.subject: Llama 3.2 1B
rows.operation_detail: Estimated feature absorption rates in the study's own trained SAEs.
rows.measure: Mean feature absorption rate by layer
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports that absorption occurs in the tested L1 and TopK SAEs.
rows.note: These SAEs were trained by the authors; exact per-layer rates are not stated.
rows.check: The 'observed' state refers to absorption, not to the V5 claim. Against V5's completeness, the authors' L1/TopK Llama SAEs show nonzero absorption, so completeness holds only partially. Drop V4.

relation.reason: The study measures feature recovery, false negatives and causal absorption, rather than merely assuming or using SAE features.

tranche.reason: The empirical absorption results and hierarchical-feature argument directly show limitations of complete dictionary-feature recovery under V5.

source_check.notes: Absorption estimates are conservative and cannot establish causal absorption beyond Gemma layer 17. The source internally conflicts on the fivefold activation comparison and on first-eight-layers versus layers 0–8.

statements.correction: For this study: Gemma-2-2B layer 3, width 16k, L0 59; latent 6510 F1 0.81; no activation on _short; latent 1085 carries a causally relevant S-probe component; absorption also occurs in tested Llama 3.2 1B L1/TopK and Qwen2 0.5B L1 SAEs. The Matryoshka, hedging, GPT-2 and Mistral comparisons are not results of this study and are outside this check.

For this study: apparent first-letter latents have false negatives; on _short, latent 6510 is inactive and the S-probe component of latent 1085 causally mediates first-letter prediction. This provides a counterexample to complete tracking by an individual apparent feature latent; stability and canonicality are not directly tested.
